y3-0: Huntington's gene therapy, a new pancreatic cancer drug, weight-loss pills, Alzheimer's blood tests, stem cells for Parkinson's and more: short, sourced summaries.
y3-4: First gene therapy for Huntington's disease awaits approval
y3-5: Huntington's disease is an inherited, progressive brain disease that affects movement, thinking and mood, and no treatment has been proven to slow its course. AMT-130, developed by uniQure, is delivered in a one-off, MRI-guided operation to the striatum, an area deep in the brain, and aims to reduce production of the faulty huntingtin protein that causes the disease. In patients who received the high dose, the disease progressed 75% more slowly at year 3 than in a comparison group; the company applied for approval in the US and the UK in September 2026.
y3-6: The results are based on a small number of patients and on a comparison with similar patients selected from disease registries rather than a placebo group. In the year 4 data released on 29 September, the difference on the main rating scale shrank to 44% and was not statistically significant, while a 61% slowing held up on a scale of daily functioning. Of those who received the high dose, 17% had a serious side effect linked to inflammation in the brain; all of these events resolved.
y3-7: Sources: uniQure, 29 September 2026 · BioPharm International, 2 September 2026
y3-8: A Parkinson's drug that works in a new way: tavapadon
y3-9: On 28 September 2026, the FDA approved AbbVie's drug tavapadon (JUVMO). Taken as a tablet once a day, it is the first drug to selectively stimulate D1 and D5, two of the dopamine receptors in the brain; the dopamine agonists used today act mainly on D2 and D3 receptors. It can be used on its own or together with levodopa. In patients taking levodopa, it increased “on” time, the good periods without troublesome involuntary movements, by 1.7 hours a day; with placebo the increase was 0.6 hours.
y3-10: The most common side effects are nausea, headache, taste disturbance, tiredness and dizziness; care is needed because of the risk of a drop in blood pressure on standing, hallucinations and impulse-control problems such as compulsive gambling. Although new drugs can make movement easier, regular exercise remains a core part of treatment for Parkinson's disease.
y3-14: First drug to replace the missing brain signal in type 1 narcolepsy
y3-15: In type 1 narcolepsy, the brain loses the cells that make orexin (hypocretin), a substance that regulates wakefulness. People struggle with irresistible sleep attacks during the day, and their muscles can suddenly go weak when they laugh or get excited (cataplexy). On 5 August 2026, the FDA approved Takeda's drug oveporexton (Orzeyful) as the first drug to stand in for the missing orexin signal. In two studies involving 273 patients, daytime wakefulness improved, and sleepiness and cataplexy attacks fell markedly.
y3-16: According to the FDA, it is the first drug to act on the underlying biology of the disease. It is taken twice a day; the most common side effects are difficulty sleeping, needing to pass urine often and increased saliva. Its safety and effectiveness in people under 18 are not yet known.
y3-18: Pancreatic cancer gets its first RAS-blocking drug
y3-19: More than 90% of pancreatic cancers carry a mutation in the RAS genes (usually KRAS) that drive tumour growth. RAS was long thought impossible to target with drugs; medicines aimed at just one specific RAS mutation were already used in lung and bowel cancer, while daraxonrasib (Rasonque), which blocks many forms of RAS at once, received FDA approval on 26 August 2026. In the RASolute 302 study of 500 patients whose pancreatic cancer had spread and who had already been treated, median survival was 6.7 months with chemotherapy and 13.2 months with daraxonrasib.
y3-20: It is taken as a tablet once a day. The most common side effects are rash, diarrhoea, mouth sores and nausea. One oncologist quoted by STAT called it the biggest advance in pancreatic cancer in decades; studies of the drug as first-line treatment are ongoing.
y3-21: Sources: FDA, 26 August 2026 · STAT
y3-23: The first PCSK9 pill for cholesterol
y3-24: PCSK9 drugs lower 'bad' (LDL) cholesterol powerfully, but until now they have only been available as injections. On 17 July 2026, the FDA approved Merck's drug enlicitide (Lipfendra) as the first PCSK9 pill, taken once a day. In two trials involving a total of 3,207 people already taking statins, LDL cholesterol at week 24 fell by 56% more than with placebo in people with, or at high risk of, cardiovascular disease, and by 59% more in people with familial hypercholesterolaemia.
y3-25: It is approved for use alongside diet and exercise. The outcome study that will show whether it reduces heart attacks and strokes has not yet been completed.
y3-28: Catching many cancers early with a single blood test: the first major results
y3-29: The NHS-Galleri study in England included 142,942 people aged 50–77 with no symptoms. Half of them had the Galleri test once a year for 3 years; the test looks in the blood for fragments of DNA shed by tumours. In the test group, about 4 times as many cancers were picked up by screening; diagnoses of stage IV cancer (cancer that has spread) fell by 14%, and more cancers were caught at an earlier stage.
y3-30: The study did not achieve a significant reduction in stage III–IV cancers, which was its main goal. It is not yet known whether earlier diagnosis helps people live longer. This test does not replace breast, cervical and bowel cancer screening.
y3-31: Sources: ASCO, June 2026 · The ASCO Post
y3-32: New weight-loss drug also eased knee osteoarthritis pain
y3-33: Retatrutide, developed by Eli Lilly, is a once-weekly injection that stimulates three hormone receptors involved in appetite and metabolism (GLP-1, GIP and glucagon) at the same time. In the TRIUMPH-4 study of 445 people with obesity and knee osteoarthritis, those on the highest dose lost an average of 28.7% of their body weight over 68 weeks; knee pain fell by 74–76% on the two doses, compared with 40.3% in the placebo group. In the TRIUMPH-1 study of 2,339 people, announced in June 2026, pain also fell by up to 73% in participants with knee osteoarthritis, although it is worth remembering that pain also fell by 40% on placebo in TRIUMPH-4.
y3-34: Retatrutide is not yet approved and is used only in clinical trials; products sold online as “retatrutide” are illegal and cannot be trusted. Nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting were common; at the highest dose, about 18% of patients stopped the drug because of side effects. In knee osteoarthritis, combining weight loss with strengthening exercises remains important.
y3-35: Sources: Eli Lilly, 11 December 2025 · Eli Lilly, 6 June 2026
y3-38: A new class of drug for hard-to-control blood pressure
y3-39: In people whose blood pressure stays high despite taking several medicines, the hormone aldosterone, which makes the body hold on to salt and water, plays an important part. AstraZeneca's drug baxdrostat (Baxfendy) received FDA approval in May 2026 as the first drug to selectively block aldosterone synthase, the enzyme that makes aldosterone. In the BaxHTN study of 796 patients taking at least two blood pressure medicines, systolic blood pressure fell by 8.7–9.8 mmHg more than with placebo at 12 weeks.
y3-40: The main side effect to watch for is a rise in potassium in the blood: potassium above 6.0 mmol/L occurred in 3% of people on the high dose and 0.4% on placebo, so potassium levels are monitored with blood tests. Do not change your blood pressure medicine without talking to your doctor. Alongside medicines, regular exercise, especially isometric exercise, has also been shown to lower blood pressure.
y3-41: Sources: New England Journal of Medicine, 2025 · Pharmacy Times, May 2026
y3-44: The first GLP-1 weight-loss pill with no food or water restrictions
y3-45: Until now, GLP-1 drugs have mostly been used as weekly injections, while oral semaglutide (the Wegovy pill), approved in December 2025, has to be taken on an empty stomach. On 1 April 2026, the FDA approved Eli Lilly's orforglipron (Foundayo) as the first GLP-1 pill that can be taken at any time of day, with no food or water restrictions. In the 72-week ATTAIN-1 study, those on the highest dose lost an average of 12.4% of their body weight, compared with 0.9% on placebo.
y3-46: It is approved for use together with a reduced-calorie diet and more physical activity. Nausea, constipation and diarrhoea are common, and the warnings about thyroid tumour risk, pancreatitis and gallbladder problems apply to this drug too. Strengthening exercises are important to reduce muscle loss while you lose weight.
y3-48: Are GLP-1 weight-loss drugs now available as pills too?
y3-49: Yes. In the US, oral semaglutide (the Wegovy pill) was approved in December 2025, followed in April 2026 by orforglipron (Foundayo), which can be taken with no food or water restrictions. In a 72-week study, average weight loss with the highest dose of orforglipron was 12.4%. These drugs are used together with diet and physical activity, under a doctor's supervision.
y3-50: Are blood tests that catch cancer early ready for use?
y3-51: Not yet. In the NHS-Galleri study of 142,942 people, the test picked up about 4 times as many cancers through screening and reduced stage IV diagnoses by 14%; however, the targeted reduction in stage III–IV cancers was not achieved, and its effect on survival is not yet known. These tests do not replace existing screening programmes.
